prize_parts.citation: For the development of palladium-catalyzed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling, a general method for constructing aryl amines

statement.case_for: Pd-catalyzed C-N coupling is the clearest case on the shortlist of a general synthetic method that changed routine practice. Aryl amines went from a harsh, substrate-limited problem to a reaction run daily in medicinal chemistry, process development and materials work. The chemistry is original at the level of ligand design (successive biaryl phosphine and hindered alkyl phosphine generations) and mechanistically well understood, so the conceptual simplicity is real. Adoption can be checked in the literature and in industrial route scouting, which is the evidence I trust most. Attribution is also unusually clean: Buchwald and Hartwig independently built the catalytic, general version, with Kosugi's tin-amide coupling a precursor rather than the general method.
statement.case_against: The 2010 prize for Pd cross-coupling will lead some colleagues to see this as the same idea applied to a different bond, and the committee may prefer a field that opens a new modality. Kosugi's precedent also leaves some priority discomfort. Against the other shortlisted fields, C-N coupling is a refinement of a recognized area, and I have to admit that its novelty is smaller than that of targeted protein degradation. Its adoption is also less visible to the wider public than that of degraders or lipid nanoparticles.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks targeted protein degradation first as a game-changer: a simple bifunctional idea that opened a new drug modality, with molecular glues linked to cereblon and several degraders in the clinic.
responses.response: I agree the concept is elegant and that it is the strongest candidate from the chemical-biology side. My reservation is about what is new chemically: the chemistry is largely linker and ligand optimization around an existing biology (E3 ligases, thalidomide's target), and the clinical proof is still prospective with no established approved degrader. I also see the three-name limit forcing an arbitrary split between the PROTAC line (Crews, Deshaies) and the cereblon glue line (Handa, Ciulli, Gray), whereas the C-N coupling credit divides cleanly. I would keep B056 as my first alternative, and I would move toward it if the committee thinks it must reward a modality over a method.

responses.point: Zou ranks the C-N coupling candidate only eighth, because it is fully mature but overlaps with the 2010 cross-coupling prize, and puts molecular-sieve catalyst design and perovskites above it.
responses.response: The overlap is the serious objection and I do not dismiss it. The 2010 prize rewarded C-C bond formation with Pd; C-N coupling needed its own ligand logic because amine binding, beta-hydride elimination and reductive elimination at C-N behave differently, and that is why the field only matured in the late 1990s. By that standard, C-N coupling is as distinct as Suzuki is from Heck. On zeolites, I accept the industrial reach, but I cannot see a single sharply defined discovery with three named people, and you say so yourself. Perovskites have unmatched speed of uptake, yet stability and lead toxicity make me think they are premature as a chemistry award.

responses.point: Sparr ranks biomolecular phase separation first as a general thermodynamic description of cell organisation, and treats degraders and ionizable lipids as strong chemical-physics cases.
responses.response: I respect the physical-chemistry argument, and I am not the right person to judge the polymer-physics content. From a molecule-making viewpoint, though, I ask what the prize would identify as a chemical discovery. The condensate field is a way of describing cells, with contested in vivo relevance, as you and Aqvist both note, and I worry that the citation would reward a concept rather than a reproducible advance. I would want to hear from you whether a Chemistry citation could be written crisply for Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen without leaving out Pappu and Mittag. Until that is clear I would put B024 behind the more mature candidates.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks nitrogenase structure and mechanism first as a physical-chemical problem of the first rank, while acknowledging that the catalytic cycle is still debated.
responses.response: Nitrogenase is a worthy subject and the FeMo-cofactor is remarkable. My concern is the one you raise yourself: the mechanism of N2 binding and reduction is unresolved, so a citation would honour structures while the chemistry that makes the enzyme interesting is not settled. I also think the credit boundary between the early structural work and the later cofactor and mechanistic work is hard to draw with five names. I would be more comfortable once the mechanism is firmer.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees C-N coupling as sufficiently distinct from the 2010 cross-coupling prize.
Exact weight to give Kosugi's precursor contribution; I rely on recollection of the history, not verification.
Whether the committee wants a method prize or a new-modality prize this year, which decides between B051 and B056.
Whether a two-person Buchwald and Hartwig prize would be seen as too narrow given Hartwig's other work (C-H borylation).
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I have no known institutional or mentoring tie to Buchwald, Hartwig or Kosugi, and my Masamune lineage does not touch this area. I sit on the committee with fellow Lund professors Linke and Sparr, but none of the credited candidates is from Lund as far as I can tell.
